sections.h2: Where is Portland and what does its layout mean for a house sale?
sections.html:
Portland sits where the Willamette and Columbia rivers meet, in Multnomah County, with small pieces of the city reaching into Clackamas and Washington counties. The city covers about 145 square miles, and the Willamette runs north through downtown and splits it into east and west halves.

Addresses are organized into six sectors: North, Northeast, Northwest, Southeast, Southwest and South. Burnside Street separates north from south. A house in Northeast near Alberta or Hollywood, one in Southeast near Hawthorne or Belmont, and one in St. Johns in the North sector can sit only a few miles apart and still draw very different buyers and repair needs.

The ground matters too. Portland is built over the Boring Lava Field, and a 2014 report flagged more than 7,000 locations at high risk for landslides and soil liquefaction in a major earthquake. Council Crest rises to 1,073 feet on the west side, while Mount Tabor, at 636 feet, is the high point east of the river. A hillside lot in the west hills and a flat lot in the east carry different foundation, drainage and insurance questions.

sections.h2: What do Portland's weather and soil do to an older house?
sections.html:
Portland has cool, wet winters and warm, dry summers, so moisture is the main wear factor on a house here. Measurable precipitation falls on about 157 days a year, and annual rainfall runs about 36.9 inches at the airport and 44.1 inches downtown.

Snow is light, about 4 inches a year, so roofs rarely fail from snow load. Long wet seasons are harder on roofing, gutters, siding and crawlspaces, and those are the items a buyer's inspector looks at closely.

Heat is part of the picture as well. The city's record high is 116 degrees, set on June 28, 2021, and about 61 days a year reach 80 degrees or higher.

  • Record low: minus 3 degrees, on February 2, 1950
  • Typical December daytime high: 46.9 degrees
  • Annual sunshine: about 2,341 hours
  • USDA hardiness zone: 8b, with parts of downtown in 9a

sections.h2: Who employs people in Portland, and why does it affect sellers?
sections.html:
Portland's job base leans on health care, technology, athletic apparel and shipping, and those employers shape which neighborhoods draw buyers. Total nonfarm employment in the city was 440,797 in 2024, and education and health services was the largest sector at 116,498 jobs.

The city's biggest employers by headcount include the following.

EmployerEmployees (2024)
Intel23,192
Oregon Health & Science University20,917
Providence Health & Services20,700
Kaiser Foundation13,086
Nike10,700
Portland Public Schools7,638

The Port of Portland handles more than 13 million tons of cargo a year and ranks third on the West Coast for export tonnage. A seller whose house is near a hospital campus, a rail stop or the river industrial areas often fields different questions from buyers than a seller in a quiet residential pocket.

sections.h2: How do I get around Portland, and does transit help a sale?
sections.html:
TriMet runs the region's buses and MAX light rail, and the Portland Streetcar is a separate city-owned system that TriMet operates under contract.

MAX has five lines, Blue, Green, Orange, Red and Yellow, covering about 60 miles with 96 stations. The first line opened in 1986 between Portland and Gresham. The Red Line reaches Portland International Airport, and TriMet carried about 66 million riders in 2025.

Bridges also shape daily travel. Downtown spans over the Willamette include Hawthorne (1910), Steel (1912), Broadway (1913), Burnside (1926), Ross Island (1926), Marquam (1966) and Tilikum Crossing (2015).

sections.h2: What is the Home Energy Score, and does my Portland house need one?
sections.html:
Most Portland houses that are publicly advertised for sale need a Home Energy Score and report before the listing goes up. The score has to appear in every ad, including the RMLS, online listings, yard signs and print, and the seller is ultimately responsible for compliance.

Sellers who sell privately with no public advertising are not covered. Other points from the city's guidance:

  • The rule follows the City of Portland boundary, not the mailing address. Some Portland addresses sit outside the city.
  • An existing score and report can be reused for up to eight years if the home has not changed.
  • Manufactured, mobile and floating homes cannot be scored and are not required to have one.
  • Sellers in certain financial distress, or with a condemned or uninhabitable house, may apply for an exemption.
  • Income-qualified sellers at or below 80 percent of Portland's area median income may be able to get a free score through Community Energy Project.

A sale that is not publicly advertised avoids the score step entirely, which matters to owners who would rather skip a pre-listing assessment. You can read the full rule on the City of Portland Home Energy Score page.

sections.h2: What happens if my Portland house has a tenant in it?
sections.html:
A Portland landlord who ends a tenancy without cause, or chooses not to renew a fixed term, generally owes the tenant relocation assistance. The city sets the amounts by unit size.

Unit sizeRelocation assistance
Studio or single room$2,900
1 bedroom$3,300
2 bedrooms$4,200
3 bedrooms or larger$4,500

Written notice has to go out at least 90 days ahead and must state the amount the tenant is eligible for. A landlord who skips the process can owe up to three times the monthly rent plus actual damages and attorney fees. One listed exemption covers a fixed-term tenancy where the tenant was told in advance that the home would be sold or permanently converted, and most exemptions need a filing with the Portland Housing Bureau.

These costs are one reason owners of occupied rentals look at a cash sale where the tenant stays in place or the timing is agreed up front. The Portland Housing Bureau page and its helpdesk at 503-823-1303 can confirm how the rules apply to your lease.

sections.h2: When are Multnomah County property taxes due on a Portland home?
sections.html:
Multnomah County bills Portland homes in three installments, due November 16, February 16 and May 17 for the 2026 tax year. Paying in full earns a 3 percent discount, and paying two-thirds earns 2 percent. A payment must be received or postmarked by the due date to keep the discount and avoid interest.

The county's Division of Assessment, Recording and Taxation sends the statements. A green statement means the owner pays directly, and a yellow one means a mortgage company may pay on the owner's behalf. Real market value for 2026 is set as of January 1, 2026, and the appeal deadline is December 31, 2026.

Oregon's Measures 5 and 50 tie taxes to an assessed value that generally cannot rise more than about 3 percent a year, even when the market value climbs faster. A long-held Portland house often has an assessed value well below its market value, so the tax bill a buyer sees on the old owner's statement can change after a sale reset. The county statement guide explains each part of the bill.

sections.h2: What must a seller disclose on an Oregon house, and how does that play out in Portland?
sections.html:
Oregon requires most sellers of residential property to give each buyer who makes a written offer a seller's property disclosure statement. The form covers title, water, sewage, insulation, structure, systems, seismic and general conditions, and the buyer has five days after delivery to revoke unless the buyer waives that right.

Some sellers use a limited exclusion and complete only Section 1 of the form. Listed exclusions include a first sale of a never-occupied dwelling, sales by a financial institution after foreclosure, sales by a court-appointed personal representative, trustee, conservator or guardian, and sales by a government agency. The statute is ORS 105.464 and 105.470.

In Portland, seismic and slope questions on that form carry real weight given the landslide and liquefaction mapping. An inherited house sold by an estate representative may qualify for the shorter form, which is one reason families handling a probate property ask about a direct sale.

sections.h2: What choices does a Portland seller have?
sections.html:
A Portland owner can list with an agent, sell without one, or sell to a cash buyer. Each path trades time, cost and certainty differently.

  • Listing: usually needs a Home Energy Score, photos, showings and a repair negotiation after inspection.
  • Selling without an agent: saves the listing-side commission but puts marketing and paperwork on you.
  • Cash sale: sold as-is, with a closing date the seller helps choose.

A cash purchase from Cash Home Buyers works from a property review and a conversation about timing. Tell us about your Portland house and we will walk through what we can do and what it would involve, with no obligation to accept.

faqs.q: Do I need a Home Energy Score to sell my Portland house?
faqs.a: Yes, if you publicly advertise the home for sale inside the City of Portland, with a few exceptions such as manufactured homes. A private sale with no public advertising is not covered. A report can be reused for up to eight years if the home has not changed.

faqs.q: When are Portland property taxes due?
faqs.a: For the 2026 tax year, Multnomah County's installments are due November 16, February 16 and May 17. Paying in full by the first date earns a 3 percent discount and paying two-thirds earns 2 percent.

faqs.q: Do I owe my tenant money if I sell my Portland rental?
faqs.a: Possibly. Ending a tenancy without cause or not renewing a fixed term in Portland generally triggers relocation assistance of $2,900 to $4,500 depending on unit size, with 90 days written notice. Some exemptions exist and most require a filing with the Portland Housing Bureau.

faqs.q: How much time does a buyer have to back out after the Oregon disclosure form?
faqs.a: A buyer has five days from delivery of the seller's disclosure statement to revoke, unless the buyer waives that right. If a seller refuses to provide the form, the buyer can revoke an offer at any time before closing.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Portland house with earthquake or landslide concerns?
faqs.a: Yes. Portland sits near the Portland Hills and East Bank faults, and a 2014 report flagged more than 7,000 high-risk locations. You answer the seismic questions on the disclosure form honestly, and a cash buyer will price the house as it stands.
